title: Quality: is this approach effective, and why?
blurb: Judge quality planning, quality control, quality assurance versus project assurance, and project acceptance in a scenario.
question: Calderbrook Council's project manager lists 'permit calls to the contact centre halved within a year' as a user's quality expectation in the project product description. Is this appropriate, and why?

teach.h: Quality you can trace, test and hand over
teach.body: Formally, the quality practice documents the user's requirements of the project's products and establishes the means by which they will be met. In plain English: write down what 'good' looks like before building, check each product against it, have someone outside the team confirm the checks are sound, and hand over only what the users accept. BL4 items test whether a project's quality choices do this, and whether you can tell quality from outcomes and benefits.

teach.caption: Quality planning produces the first three; quality control applies them; acceptance closes the loop (fig 8.1).

head: Statement
It is a...
rows: Easy to use on a phone
Permit calls halved in a year
teach.caption: Expectations and acceptance criteria sit in the project product description; specifications sit in each product description. Outcomes and benefits belong to the business case practice.

teach.body: Quality planning captures the user's quality expectations and prioritized acceptance criteria in the project product description during starting up, then produces the quality management approach and product descriptions. The PPD should identify all major products so out-of-scope requirements do not creep into lower-level product descriptions. Requirements will change; when lower-level planning would change the baselined PID, the change goes through the issue management approach.

Quality control carries out the quality methods and records each activity and result, typically pass or fail, in the quality register; a failed check may be repeated if a pass is expected after rework, and the records feed the end stage and end project reports. Acceptance of the project product typically transfers ownership and responsibility from the project or supplier to the project board on behalf of the users. Acceptance is confirmed in closing a project.

teach.text: Classic traps. An outcome or benefit, such as 'more residents apply online' or 'calls halved', is not a user's quality expectation or acceptance criterion. And quality assurance is not project assurance: quality assurance sits outside the project management team and checks the quality controls; project assurance works for the board and is independent of the PM but not of the project.

teach.body: Hannah Okoro, the project manager, records in the project product description that the service must meet WCAG 2.2 AA and pass an independent accessibility audit and an IT health check before go-live. Kestrel Lane's team tests each feature with real users in sprint reviews and logs results in the quality register. Priya Lal, the council's digital assurance lead, who has no role in the project team, checks that the planned tests meet the council's service standard: quality assurance.

items: Is the statement about the product, or about its effect? Effects are outcomes or benefits.
Are checks planned in proportion to the delivery approach and product characteristics?
Are results recorded in the quality register, with fails handled and retested?
Is assurance independent: QA outside the PMT, project assurance independent of the PM?
Is acceptance against the agreed criteria, transferring responsibility for the users?
Outcomes and benefits are not user's quality expectations or acceptance criteria (8.1.1, 5.1).
Tailor quality activities to the delivery approach and product characteristics (tab 8.3).
Changes to the baselined PID from lower-level planning go through the issue approach (8.2.1.6).
Quality assurance is independent of the PMT; project assurance is independent of the PM (8.2.3).
Acceptance transfers responsibility from the project or supplier to the board for the users (8.3.1.3).

summary: You can now judge whether quality planning, quality control, assurance and acceptance are applied effectively. You can separate quality expectations from outcomes and benefits, and quality assurance from project assurance.

A.q: Calderbrook Borough Council is starting up its Permits Online project. Project manager Hannah Okoro writes in the project product description, under user's quality expectations: 'Permit calls to the contact centre halved within a year of launch.' What is this statement?
options: A user's quality expectation, so the PPD is right
An acceptance criterion, so it belongs in the PPD
A benefit, so it belongs in the business case
A quality specification for a product description
A.why: A benefit is a measurable improvement resulting from an outcome. Halving calls is a benefit, recorded under expected benefits in the business case, not a statement about the product's quality (5.1, 8.1.1).

whyNot.0: A user's quality expectation is about the quality expected of the project product, not the effect of using it.
whyNot.1: Acceptance criteria are measurable attributes the product must have to be accepted; call volumes are a later result.
whyNot.3: Quality specifications are measures for a specific product, not organization-wide improvements.

A.q: On Calderbrook's Permits Online project, Priya Lal, the council's digital assurance lead, has no role in the project management team. She reviews whether the project's planned accessibility audit, IT health check and user testing are appropriate against the council's digital service standard. What is she performing?
options: Quality assurance
Project assurance
Quality control
Quality planning
A.why: Quality assurance is performed independently of the project management team, for example by a business function, and checks that the project's quality controls are appropriate (8.2.3).

whyNot.1: Project assurance is done on behalf of the project board as part of the project; Priya sits outside the project management team.
whyNot.2: Quality control is carrying out the checks on products, not reviewing whether the checks are appropriate.
whyNot.3: Quality planning defines the expectations, criteria and approach; Priya is reviewing them independently.

A.q: Calderbrook's Permits Online is in its discovery and alpha stage. The first accessibility test of the application form fails two checks. Kestrel Lane fixes the faults, expects a pass and repeats the test, which then passes. Where should both test results be recorded?
options: The product register
The issue register
The lessons log
The quality register
A.why: Quality control results are recorded in the quality register, typically as pass or fail, and a failed check may be repeated if a pass is expected (8.3.1.2).

whyNot.0: The product register lists products and their status, not the results of each check.
whyNot.1: The issue register records formal issues; a failed check followed by rework and a pass is recorded as quality activity.
whyNot.2: The lessons log records lessons, not individual test results.

B.q: Calderbrook's Permits Online project is finishing its public beta. The service is ready to pass from the project and Kestrel Lane to the council's parking services team. To whom does acceptance of the project product transfer ownership and responsibility?
options: Kestrel Lane Digital, as the supplier
The project board, on behalf of the users
Hannah Okoro, as the project manager
The council's project management office
B.why: Acceptance typically transfers ownership and responsibility from the project or supplier to the project board on behalf of the user (8.3.1.3).

whyNot.0: Responsibility moves away from the supplier on acceptance, not to it.
whyNot.2: The project manager's role ends at closure; responsibility does not transfer to the PM.
whyNot.3: The PMO may provide project support, but it does not take ownership of the product.

B.q: Calderbrook's project board wants confidence, on its own behalf and independent of project manager Hannah Okoro, that Permits Online is being run correctly and that its quality controls are being followed. What should the board put in place?
options: Quality control by Kestrel Lane's testers
Project support from the council's PMO
Project assurance appointed by the board
Quality planning in the project product description
B.why: Project assurance is the board's responsibility, confirming the project is being conducted correctly, independent of the PM but not of the project (8.2.3, 6.2.4).

whyNot.0: Quality control checks products; it is done by the teams, not independently for the board.
whyNot.1: Project support works for the PM and must be kept separate from assurance.
whyNot.3: Quality planning defines expectations and criteria; it does not give the board independent confidence.

B.q: While writing product descriptions in the discovery stage, Kestrel Lane adds a requirement for a residents' parking map feature that is not among the major products in Calderbrook's baselined project product description. What should project manager Hannah Okoro do?
options: Handle it through the issue management approach
Keep it, because product descriptions add detail
Record it in the quality register as a new method
Let the team absorb it within work package tolerance
B.why: Changes to the baselined PID arising from lower-level planning go through the issue management approach; the PPD's list of major products keeps requirements within approved scope (8.2.1.1, 8.2.1.6).

whyNot.1: Product descriptions add detail to agreed products; they should not add new out-of-scope products.
whyNot.2: The quality register records quality activities, not new requirements.
whyNot.3: A new feature changes the baseline, so it needs change control rather than absorption by the team.

C.q: Calderbrook's supplier, Kestrel Lane, builds Permits Online in two-week sprints. Hannah Okoro agrees that each sprint's features are tested with real residents, including people who use assistive technology, at the sprint review, instead of a formal written quality review for every screen. How well does this apply the 'quality' practice, and why?
options: Well, because quality work should suit the delivery approach
Well, because the quality register summarizes all activities
Poorly, because every product needs a formal quality review
Poorly, because the supplier's testers should run all the tests
C.why: Tailoring the quality practice means requiring only those quality activities appropriate to the delivery approach and the product characteristics (tab 8.3).

whyNot.1: It is true the register summarizes quality activities, but that does not explain why sprint-review testing is suitable.
whyNot.2: Quality methods are chosen to suit the product and approach; a formal written review is not required for every product.
whyNot.3: Users, including residents, can take part in quality checks; the council's standard requires testing with real users.

C.q: To save money on Calderbrook's Permits Online project, project manager Hannah Okoro proposes that she checks, on the board's behalf, that the agreed quality controls are being followed by Kestrel Lane's team. Is this an appropriate application of the 'quality' practice, and why?
options: Yes, because the PM ensures team managers apply quality controls
Yes, because the PMO already provides support to the project
No, because quality assurance must be performed by the supplier
No, because project assurance must be independent of the PM
C.why: Project assurance confirms for the board that the project is being conducted correctly, independent of the project manager; the PM cannot perform it (8.2.3).

whyNot.0: The PM does make sure controls are applied, but checking them on the board's behalf is assurance, which must be independent of the PM.
whyNot.1: Project support is the PM's responsibility and must be kept separate from assurance.
whyNot.2: Quality assurance is a business or programme function outside the project management team, not the supplier.

C.q: Calderbrook's private beta in the Old Town ward was well received. The executive proposes launching Permits Online across the whole borough before the independent accessibility audit report arrives, even though passing the audit is one of the acceptance criteria. Is this an appropriate application of the 'quality' practice, and why?
options: Yes, because good beta feedback shows expectations have been met
Yes, because requirements will change during the project anyway
No, because go-live decisions belong to the supplier's director
No, because acceptance criteria must be met before users accept
C.why: Acceptance criteria are the prioritized, measurable criteria the project product must meet before the user will accept it (8.1.1).

whyNot.0: Positive feedback is welcome, but it does not replace an agreed acceptance criterion.
whyNot.1: It is true requirements change, but changes are controlled; an agreed criterion cannot simply be skipped.
whyNot.2: Acceptance is for the board on behalf of the users, not the supplier.

reteach.title: Before, during and after the build
reteach.question: What should happen before Calderbrook builds anything, while it builds, and before it hands over?

blocks.body: Before: agree what 'good' looks like (expectations and acceptance criteria in the PPD, a quality approach, product descriptions with specifications). During: check each product against its specification and record every check in the quality register, while someone outside the team confirms the checks are sound. Before handover: confirm the acceptance criteria are met, so responsibility can pass to the board on behalf of the users.

items.label: PPD: WCAG 2.2 AA, audit, health check
User tests logged in quality register

blocks.text: If the statement describes what happens AFTER people use the product (calls fall, residents switch online), it is an outcome or benefit, not a quality expectation.

explain.body: User's quality expectations: high-level statement about the project product, in the PPD. Acceptance criteria: prioritized, measurable criteria the product must meet to be accepted, in the PPD. Quality specifications: measures for each product, in its product description.

test.q: Calderbrook's PPD states that Permits Online must pass an independent accessibility audit and an IT health check before go-live. What are these?
options: Expected benefits
Acceptance criteria
Quality methods
Outcomes
test.why: They are measurable conditions the project product must meet before it is accepted: acceptance criteria in the PPD (8.1.1).

whyNot.0: Benefits are measurable improvements from outcomes.
whyNot.2: Quality methods are how checks are done; here the stem states conditions for acceptance.
whyNot.3: Outcomes are results of change in behaviour.

explain.body: Carrying out the quality methods on products and recording each activity and result in the quality register. A failed check may be repeated if a pass is expected; the records feed end stage and end project reports.

test.q: Calderbrook's quality register shows all of discovery's planned checks with their results. Which report draws on these records at the end of the stage?
options: The checkpoint report
The end stage report
The issue report
The exception report
test.why: Quality register records feed the end stage and end project reports (8.3.1.2).

whyNot.0: Checkpoint reports are the team manager's periodic status reports.
whyNot.2: Issue reports describe an individual issue.
whyNot.3: Exception reports describe a forecast tolerance breach.

explain.body: Quality assurance is a planned, systematic activity, typically by a business or programme function outside the project management team, checking that quality controls are appropriate. Project assurance is the board's responsibility, independent of the PM but not of the project.

test.q: Calderbrook's internal digital assurance function, outside the project management team, reviews whether Permits Online's testing approach is fit for purpose. Is this quality assurance or project assurance?
options: Project assurance, as it serves the board
Quality control, as it reviews testing
Quality assurance, as it is outside the PMT
Project support, as it advises on tools
test.why: Quality assurance is performed independently of the project management team and checks that the project's quality controls are appropriate (8.2.3).

whyNot.0: Project assurance works for the board within the project.
whyNot.1: Quality control checks products, not the testing approach.
whyNot.3: Project support is part of the project and works for the PM.

explain.body: Acceptance of the project product typically transfers ownership and responsibility from the project or supplier to the project board on behalf of the users. It is confirmed in closing a project against the acceptance criteria in the PPD.

test.q: In which process does Calderbrook's project manager confirm acceptance of the Permits Online service?
options: Controlling a stage
Managing a stage boundary
Directing a project
Closing a project
test.why: 'Confirm project acceptance' is an activity of closing a project (19.4.3).

whyNot.0: Controlling a stage receives completed work packages.
whyNot.1: Managing a stage boundary prepares the next stage.
whyNot.2: Directing a project authorizes closure; the PM confirms acceptance in closing.
